title: Working at Height
introduction: Falls from height are the single biggest killer in the UK construction industry. Last year, falls accounted for the largest proportion of fatal injuries to construction workers. The frightening thing is that most of these deaths were preventable. Today we are going to talk about what we need to do every time we work at height — no matter how quick the job seems.
key_message: Falls from height kill more construction workers than anything else. Every job at height needs planning — every time.
key_points: The law — The Work at Height Regulations 2005 apply to any work where a person could fall and injure themselves — that includes work below ground level too. There is no minimum height. Even a fall from 1 metre can kill.

Hierarchy of control — First — avoid working at height if you can. Second — use collective protection like scaffold and edge protection. Third — use personal protection like a harness. A harness is always a last resort, not a first choice.

Inspect before you use — Check scaffold before you use it — is the CISRS tag current? Are all boards, guard rails and toe boards in place? Check your harness before you put it on — look at every stitch, buckle and D-ring. Check your ladder — no cracks, no missing rungs, feet in good condition.

Ladders — the rules — Ladders are for access and short duration tasks only — maximum 30 minutes. Angle is one out for every four up. Tie at the top where possible. If not, have someone foot it throughout. Maintain three points of contact at all times.

Never take shortcuts — It is never worth the risk to stand on a bucket, lean out beyond a guardrail or skip an inspection because the job will only take five minutes. The person who fell last month thought the same thing.

Guard rails, mid-rails and toe boards in place
Harnesses being worn and clipped to anchor points
Correct ladder angle — one out for every four up
Exclusion zones below working areas
Tool tethers on all hand tools used at height

Guard rails removed or tied back

title: Manual Handling
introduction: Manual handling injuries — bad backs, pulled muscles, damaged joints — are the most common reason construction workers take time off work. In fact, over a third of all workplace injuries involve manual handling. The good news is that the vast majority are preventable. Today we are going to remind ourselves of how to handle materials safely and what to do when a load is too much for one person.
key_message: Manual handling injuries are the most common cause of absence in construction. Most can be prevented by thinking before you lift.
key_points: The manual handling assessment — Before lifting anything, consider four things — the Task (what are you doing?), the Individual (are you fit to do it?), the Load (how heavy and awkward is it?) and the Environment (is the floor clear? Is there enough space?). This is the TILE approach.

Avoid it where possible — Can you use a mechanical aid instead? A sack truck, pallet truck, hoist, forklift or telehandler? Using machinery is always better than manual handling. Never manually handle anything that a machine can do safely.

The correct technique — Feet shoulder-width apart, close to the load. Bend your knees, not your back. Get a firm grip. Keep the load close to your body. Lift smoothly — do not jerk. Turn with your feet, not your back. Set down carefully.

Team lifts — Any load over 25kg should be a team lift or mechanically assisted. For team lifts, one person leads and calls the movements. Everyone lifts and sets down at the same time. Agree the route before you start.

Cumulative risk — It is not just one heavy lift that causes injury. Repeating the same movement all day — laying blocks, digging, carrying bricks — puts enormous strain on your body. Rotate tasks, take regular breaks and stretch.

Clear routes before moving loads

title: Personal Protective Equipment
introduction: PPE — Personal Protective Equipment — is there to protect you when everything else has been done. It is not a substitute for good risk control. But when you need it, you really need it. Today we are going to talk about the PPE required on this site, how to check it is fit for purpose and what to do if it is damaged or does not fit properly.
key_message: PPE is your last line of defence. It only works if it fits correctly, is in good condition and is actually worn.
key_points: PPE is a legal requirement — The Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 2022 require employers to provide suitable PPE and employees to use it correctly. Refusing to wear PPE on site is a disciplinary matter and can result in removal from site.

Mandatory PPE on this site — As a minimum on this site: safety helmet, high-visibility clothing, safety footwear with steel toecap and midsole, and gloves for handling materials. Additional PPE will be required for specific tasks — check your RAMS or ask your supervisor.

Check it before you use it — Inspect your PPE at the start of every day. Check your helmet for cracks — especially inside the shell. Check your harness stitching and buckles. Check your safety boots for sole separation. If in doubt, replace it.

Fit matters — PPE that does not fit correctly does not protect you. Helmets must be adjusted to fit. Gloves must allow you to grip safely. Respirators must be face-fit tested. If your PPE does not fit, report it to your supervisor and get a replacement.

Replace it — Helmets must be replaced after any significant impact — even if you cannot see damage. Harnesses involved in a fall must be taken out of service immediately. Do not use PPE past its expiry date or manufacturer's recommended service life.

title: Slips, Trips and Falls
introduction: You might think slips and trips are minor — a twisted ankle, a bruised knee. But they cause thousands of serious injuries every year, including broken bones, head injuries and fatalities when they happen at height or near moving plant. The biggest cause is simple — an untidy, poorly managed site. Today we are going to talk about how we keep this site slip and trip free.
key_message: Slips and trips cause more injuries on construction sites than almost anything else. A tidy site is a safe site.
key_points: Housekeeping is everyone's job — Do not walk past a hazard and leave it for someone else. If you create a slip or trip hazard — clean it up. If you see one that is not yours — deal with it or report it. A tidy site is not just about appearances, it saves lives.

Common causes — Trailing cables, offcuts of timber and steel, spilt materials, wet and muddy footpaths, uneven ground, missing trench covers, poor lighting, and debris on stairs and walkways. All of these are preventable.
Footwear — Safety footwear must have a good tread and anti-slip sole. Worn soles are as dangerous as no soles at all. Do not wear smooth-soled boots on site. Report worn footwear to your supervisor.

Wet and muddy conditions — Construction sites are muddy. Mud is a serious slip hazard. Keep walkways and access routes as clear as possible. Use duck boards on muddy routes. Clean boots before using stairways or ladders.

Lighting — Good lighting is essential to see where you are walking. In winter months and in enclosed spaces, make sure lighting is adequate before starting work. Report broken or inadequate lighting immediately.

title: COSHH — Hazardous Substances
introduction: COSHH stands for Control of Substances Hazardous to Health. On a construction site we work with hazardous substances every single day — cement, solvents, adhesives, paints, dust from cutting wood or stone, diesel fumes from plant. Many of these cause health problems that do not show up immediately. Occupational disease from construction — lung disease, skin disease, cancer — kills more construction workers every year than accidents do. Today we are going to talk about how we protect ourselves.
key_message: Hazardous substances cause serious long-term health damage. Protect yourself — the effects may not show for years.
key_points: What is a hazardous substance? — Anything that can harm your health through breathing it in, skin contact, ingestion or injection. On site this includes: cement and concrete dust, silica dust from cutting stone or block, wood dust, solvents in paints and adhesives, asbestos, welding fumes, diesel exhaust and many others.

Silica dust — the hidden killer — Silica dust from cutting, grinding or drilling stone, brick, block and concrete causes silicosis — an irreversible, fatal lung disease. There is no cure. Any dry cutting of these materials without dust suppression or RPE puts you at serious risk.

Dermatitis from cement — Wet cement is highly alkaline and causes chemical burns and dermatitis. Over time it sensitises your skin so that even small amounts cause severe reactions. Wear chemical resistant gloves, use barrier cream and wash hands thoroughly.

The hierarchy of control — First — eliminate the substance. Second — substitute for something less harmful. Third — enclose or extract the substance at source (LEV). Fourth — use RPE as a last resort. RPE alone is not enough — it must be combined with other controls.

Read the safety data sheet — Every hazardous substance on site must have a Safety Data Sheet (SDS). These tell you what the hazards are, what PPE to use and what to do in an emergency. Ask your supervisor if you cannot find the SDS for a product you are using.

title: Excavations Safety
audience: Groundworkers, plant operators, all working near excavations
introduction: Excavation collapses kill construction workers in the UK every year. A cubic metre of soil weighs over a tonne. When an excavation collapses it happens fast — there is no warning, no time to react and no way to escape. The person is buried instantly. Rescue is extremely difficult. Today we are talking about how we make sure everyone working near excavations goes home safe.
key_message: An unsupported excavation can collapse without warning and bury a person within seconds. Never enter an unsafe excavation.
key_points: The 1.2 metre rule — Any excavation deeper than 1.2 metres must be either battered back to a safe angle, benched in steps, or supported with trench sheets, drag boxes or proprietary support systems. There are no exceptions. Soil type affects how steep the safe angle is — sandy or made ground requires shallower battering.

Services — stop before you dig — Always obtain service drawings before excavating. Always carry out a CAT and Genny survey on every trench line before the machine starts. Mark all services. Hand dig within 500mm of any marked service. Striking a gas main or high voltage cable can be fatal.

Daily inspections — Excavations must be inspected at the start of every shift, after any rainfall and after any event that might affect stability. The inspection must be carried out by a competent person and recorded in writing. If in doubt — do not enter.

Protect others — Excavations left open overnight must be fenced with Heras fencing — not just barriers or cones — and signed. Spoil must be kept at least 1 metre from the edge of the excavation. Vehicle exclusion zones must be enforced.

If it collapses — Do not jump in to rescue. This causes multiple casualties. Call 999 immediately. Establish an exclusion zone. Only trained persons with correct rescue equipment should attempt entry.

title: Fire Safety on Site
introduction: Construction sites are one of the highest fire risk environments there is. Combustible materials everywhere, hot works, temporary electrical supplies, fuel storage. A fire can spread incredibly fast on a site — particularly in timber-framed structures or buildings under fit-out. Today we are going to make sure every person on this site knows exactly what to do if a fire starts.
key_message: Construction sites are high fire risk environments. Know what to do before a fire starts — not after.
key_points: Prevention is everything — Most site fires are preventable. Keep combustible waste — timber off-cuts, packaging, shavings — cleared to skips daily. Do not allow combustibles to accumulate in any area. Store fuels and gases correctly — upright, in a ventilated cage, away from ignition sources.

Hot works — Any hot works — welding, grinding, disc cutting, gas torch — requires a hot works permit. The area must be cleared of combustibles beforehand. A fire extinguisher must be within reach. After completing hot works, a fire watch must be maintained for 30 minutes. Many site fires start from smouldering that begins long after the work is done.

Know the muster point — The muster point for this site is [INSERT LOCATION]. Every person on site must know where it is. If you are new to this site today — find out before you start work. In the event of a fire alarm, evacuate immediately. Do not collect tools or equipment.

Extinguisher types — Know which extinguisher to use. CO2 (black label) — electrical fires. Dry powder (blue label) — gas and liquid fires. Water (red) — general materials. Never use water on electrical fires. Fire extinguishers are for small, contained fires only. If in doubt, get out.

Raise the alarm first — If you discover a fire — raise the alarm first. Shout, activate the alarm, tell others. Then call 999. Only then consider tackling a small fire with an extinguisher — if it is safe to do so. Never put yourself between a fire and your exit route.

Hot works permit in place before welding or gas torch work

title: Electrical Safety
introduction: Electrical accidents on construction sites cause deaths, serious burns and fires. The danger is invisible — you cannot see it, smell it or hear it until it is too late. There are two main electrical risks on a construction site: contact with overhead or underground power lines during groundworks and plant operation, and contact with live electrical supplies through damaged tools, temporary supplies or incomplete electrical installations. Today we are covering what everyone needs to know.
key_message: You cannot see electricity. Never assume a cable or circuit is dead — always test first.
key_points: Always assume it is live — Never assume a cable, circuit or piece of electrical equipment is dead. Always test before touching. Use a GS38 compliant voltage tester — test the tester on a known live source before and after testing the unknown circuit. If you are not a qualified electrician, do not touch electrical equipment beyond plugging in tools.

110V on site — All portable electrical equipment on site should be 110V centre-tapped to earth — not 230V domestic supply. 110V significantly reduces the risk of fatality if contact is made. Check that all your equipment is 110V before using it on site.

Inspect before you use — Check every electrical tool before you plug it in. Look for damage to the cable — cuts, abrasions or bare wires. Check the plug — no cracked casing, no missing pins. Check the body of the tool. If anything is damaged, take it out of service immediately and report it.

Underground and overhead services — Before any excavation, a CAT and Genny survey must be done. Before any work near overhead lines, the lines must be identified and a safe working distance established. Electricity can arc — you do not have to touch a high voltage line to be killed by it.

RCDs — All temporary electrical supplies must be protected by a Residual Current Device (RCD). Check that the RCD is in circuit and test it regularly using the test button. An RCD cuts the power in milliseconds if a fault is detected — it can save your life.

title: Hot Works Safety
audience: All operatives carrying out or working near hot works
introduction: Hot works — welding, grinding, cutting with disc cutters, gas torch work — are one of the leading causes of serious fires on construction sites and in occupied buildings. The dangerous thing about hot works fires is that they often start long after the work is finished. Smouldering in timber, insulation or roofing felt can start a fire hours later. Today we are going to cover the hot works permit process and what every person involved in hot works must do.
key_message: Most hot works fires start after the job is finished. A 30-minute fire watch is not optional — it is essential.
key_points: What counts as hot works — Any activity that produces a flame, sparks or sufficient heat to ignite materials. This includes: welding and cutting, disc grinding, disc cutting, soldering torch, bitumen boiler work, gas torch on flat roofing. If it creates heat or sparks — it needs a hot works permit.

The hot works permit — A hot works permit must be completed and signed before any hot works begin. The permit confirms that the area has been prepared — combustibles removed, fire extinguisher in place, fire watch arranged. The permit is site-specific and time-limited. Never carry out hot works without a valid permit.

Prepare the area — Remove all combustible materials from a minimum 5-metre radius of the hot works area. Cover what cannot be removed with fire-resistant blankets. Check above, below and behind — sparks and heat travel in all directions. Wet down timber and combustible surfaces where possible.

During the works — Keep a fire extinguisher within arm's reach at all times. Never leave hot works unattended. If the work must stop — extinguish or isolate the heat source. Check for ignition in surrounding materials every 10 minutes during the work.

The 30-minute fire watch — After completing all hot works, a fire watch must be maintained for a minimum of 30 minutes. The fire watch person stays in the area and monitors for smouldering or fire. They must have a fire extinguisher. They cannot leave the area early for any reason.

title: Plant and Vehicle Safety
introduction: Plant and vehicle movements on construction sites cause fatalities every year. People are struck by reversing vehicles, run over by dumpers, hit by slewing excavators. The vast majority of these incidents happen because pedestrians were in areas where plant was operating. Today we are covering how plant and people are kept separate on this site and what every person needs to know.
key_message: Being struck by moving plant is one of the most common causes of fatal injury on construction sites. If you cannot see the operator — the operator cannot see you.
key_points: Segregation is everything — Plant and pedestrians must be kept separate wherever possible using physical barriers — not just painted lines or cones. If you are on foot, stay on pedestrian routes. Never take a shortcut through a plant operating area. If there is no physical barrier, wait until the plant has stopped before crossing.

The danger zones — Every piece of plant has danger zones — areas where the operator has limited or no visibility. For an excavator, this is behind and to the sides. For a dumper, it is directly in front and behind. For a telehandler, it is anywhere the load obscures the view. Never position yourself in a blind spot.

Banksman — When plant is reversing or operating in an area where pedestrians may be present, a trained banksman must be in place. The banksman gives clear, agreed signals to the operator. If you are banksman — never stand behind reversing plant. Stand where you can see both the operator and the hazard.

Pre-use checks — Plant operators must complete a pre-use inspection at the start of every shift. This includes checking brakes, lights, horn, mirrors, ROPS/FOPS, seatbelt and reversing alarm. If a defect is found, the machine must not be used until it is repaired.

Speed limits — Site speed limits must be observed by all vehicles — including delivery lorries and personal vehicles. The limit on this site is [INSERT SPEED LIMIT]. Speed limits are not advisory. Speeding on a construction site is a disciplinary matter.

title: Noise and Dust
introduction: Noise and dust are two of the biggest causes of occupational disease in the construction industry. Noise-induced hearing loss affects hundreds of thousands of workers in the UK and it is permanent — there is no cure. Silicosis and other lung diseases from dust kill construction workers every year. The worst thing about both is that the damage builds up slowly and you do not notice it until it is too late. Today we are talking about what we do on this site to protect ourselves.
key_message: Hearing loss and lung disease from construction work are permanent. Protect yourself now — the damage cannot be undone.
key_points: Noise — the risks — Exposure to loud noise over time permanently damages the hair cells in your ears that convert sound to signals. Once destroyed they do not regenerate. Symptoms include ringing in the ears (tinnitus) and difficulty hearing speech in background noise. Power tools, disc cutters, jackhammers and compactors all produce dangerous noise levels.

Noise — the controls — Ear protection zones are established wherever noise levels exceed 85dB — roughly the level of a busy road. Inside these zones, ear protection must be worn at all times. Ear defenders must be the correct rating for the noise level and must be worn correctly — touching skin all around the seal.

Dust — the risks — Silica dust from cutting, grinding or drilling stone, brick, block and concrete causes silicosis — a fatal, irreversible lung disease. Wood dust — particularly hardwood and MDF — causes nasal cancer. General construction dust causes asthma and other respiratory disease. Short-term exposure causes long-term damage.

Dust — the controls — Wet cutting wherever possible — water suppression on disc cutters and angle grinders. Local exhaust ventilation (LEV) — dust extraction attached to power tools. Respiratory protective equipment — minimum FFP2 for general dust, FFP3 for silica dust and wood dust. All three together, not just one.

Health surveillance — If you work regularly with dusty materials or noisy equipment, you may be subject to health surveillance — regular hearing and lung function tests. This is a legal requirement for employers where workers are regularly exposed above action values. If you have noticed changes in your hearing or breathing, report it now.

Wet cutting being used to suppress silica dust
Dust extraction attached to power tools

title: Asbestos Awareness
audience: All site operatives — particularly those working on older buildings
introduction: Asbestos is the single biggest cause of work-related deaths in the UK, killing around 5,000 people every year. Most of these are construction workers who were exposed to asbestos decades ago. There is no safe level of asbestos exposure. It causes mesothelioma — a fatal cancer — and asbestosis. Because buildings built or refurbished before 2000 may still contain asbestos, construction workers are still being exposed today. This talk is about recognising the risk and knowing what to do.
key_message: Asbestos kills more construction workers than any other single cause. If you think you have found it — stop work immediately.
key_points: Where asbestos is found — Any building built or refurbished before 2000 may contain asbestos. Common locations: roof sheets and tiles, floor tiles and adhesive, ceiling tiles, insulation on pipes and boilers, textured coatings (Artex), fire protection boards, rope seals in boilers, insulation boards (AIB), guttering and drainpipes, gaskets.

Types of asbestos — Three main types: white (chrysotile), brown (amosite) and blue (crocidolite). Blue and brown are the most dangerous but all types are hazardous. You cannot identify asbestos by colour alone. Do not try to identify it — assume it is asbestos and act accordingly.

The asbestos survey — Before any refurbishment, maintenance or demolition work on a pre-2000 building, a Type R (Refurbishment and Demolition) asbestos survey must be completed by an accredited surveyor. The survey identifies the location, condition and type of any ACMs. Ask to see it before you start work.

Stop if you find it — If you disturb or suspect you have found asbestos — STOP WORK immediately. Do not disturb it further. Leave the area and prevent others from entering. Tell the site manager or your supervisor immediately. Do not attempt to remove or bag it yourself unless you are licensed to do so.

Licensed and non-licensed work — Some asbestos removal requires a licensed contractor — this includes sprayed asbestos, asbestos insulation and Asbestos Insulating Board (AIB). Other lower-risk materials can be removed under non-licensed notifiable (NNLW) conditions with the correct controls. No asbestos removal without the correct authorisation.

title: Near Miss Reporting
introduction: A near miss is any unplanned event that could have resulted in injury, illness or damage but did not. The tool that fell off the scaffold and missed someone by a foot. The telehandler that nearly clipped the pedestrian route. The scaffold board that shifted as someone stepped on it. Every near miss is a warning — a chance to prevent a serious accident before it happens. Research shows that for every serious accident, there are dozens of near misses and hundreds of unsafe conditions. Report them all.
key_message: A near miss is an accident waiting to happen. Report every one — no blame, just action.
key_points: Why reporting matters — Near miss reporting saves lives. When a near miss is reported and investigated, the underlying cause can be identified and fixed before someone gets hurt. Sites that have a strong near miss reporting culture have fewer serious accidents. Failing to report a near miss that later becomes a serious accident is a missed opportunity that could have saved a life.

No blame culture — Near misses must be reported without fear of blame or disciplinary action. The point is to learn from them and fix the problem — not to punish the person involved. If people are afraid to report, near misses stay hidden and accidents follow. If you see something that should not be happening, report it.

How to report on this site — Near misses can be reported to your supervisor verbally, in writing using the site near miss form or via [INSERT SITE REPORTING METHOD]. Reports will be reviewed by the site manager within 24 hours. Where action is required, it will be taken and fed back to the team.

What happens after a report — Every near miss report is investigated to find the root cause. Was it a behavioural issue? A system or process issue? An equipment or site condition issue? Action is taken to prevent recurrence. The outcome is shared with the team — so everyone learns.

Unsafe conditions are near misses too — You do not have to witness an incident to submit a near miss report. Spotting an unsafe condition — a missing guard rail, a damaged scaffold board, an unmarked trench — is equally valuable. Report what you see. It will be acted on.

title: Confined Spaces
audience: Groundworkers, drainage operatives, anyone working in manholes or restricted spaces
introduction: A confined space is any enclosed or partially enclosed space that is not designed for continuous occupancy and has restricted means of entry or exit. On a construction site this includes manholes, inspection chambers, sewers, excavations, tanks, ducts and some roof voids. Confined spaces kill people in two ways — toxic or oxygen-depleted atmospheres and physical entrapment. Critically, many deaths in confined spaces are rescuers who entered without correct equipment. Today we are covering what every person on this site needs to know.
key_message: Most confined space deaths are rescuers — not the original casualty. Never enter to rescue without the correct equipment and training.
key_points: The hazards — Oxygen deficiency — oxygen levels below 19.5% cause unconsciousness rapidly and death. Toxic gases — hydrogen sulphide (H2S) from sewage, carbon monoxide (CO) from plant exhaust, methane from decomposing organic matter. All of these are colourless and may be odourless. You cannot detect them without a gas monitor.

Classify before you enter — Confined spaces are classified by risk level. Class 1 — low risk, short entry with monitoring. Class 2 — medium risk, permit to work required. Class 3 — high risk, full rescue team required. The risk class determines the procedure. If you are not sure — treat it as Class 3.

The permit to work — A confined space permit to work must be completed before entry into any Class 2 or 3 confined space. The permit confirms that the space has been tested, the rescue plan is in place and the entry team is adequately trained and equipped. No permit — no entry.

Gas monitoring — A calibrated 4-gas monitor must be used to test the atmosphere before entry — oxygen, carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulphide and lower explosive limit. The monitor must be lowered into the space on a rope before any person enters. Monitoring must continue throughout the entry.

Never rescue without equipment — If someone collapses in a confined space, the instinctive reaction is to go in after them. This reaction has caused more confined space deaths than the original incident. Call 999 immediately. Ventilate where possible. Use the rescue tripod and lifeline. Wait for the fire service. Entering without SCBA and rescue equipment will kill you.

title: Welfare and Site Hygiene
introduction: Welfare and hygiene on a construction site is a legal requirement — not a luxury. The Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 set minimum standards for welfare facilities. Today we are going to cover what you should expect on this site and why it matters for your health and the health of your colleagues.
key_message: Good welfare and hygiene on site protects your health and the health of everyone around you.
key_points: Minimum welfare requirements — CDM 2015 requires: flushing toilets (or suitable chemical equivalent), washbasins with hot and cold water, soap and drying facilities, a rest area with facilities to warm food and make hot drinks, changing facilities where operatives have to wear site clothing, and drinking water. These are legal minimums — not optional.

Hand washing — Washing your hands properly is one of the most important things you can do on a construction site. Cement and lime cause dermatitis over time. Silica dust and lead from old paint can be ingested. Wash hands thoroughly before eating, drinking, smoking or using the toilet. Use the soap and hot water provided — not just a wipe on your trousers.

Skin care — Dermatitis — inflamed, cracked, painful skin — affects thousands of construction workers. Once sensitised, even small amounts of cement, solvents or other chemicals cause severe reactions. Use the barrier cream provided before work, wash thoroughly during and after, and apply moisturiser at the end of the day. Report any skin problems early.

Food and drink on site — Never eat, drink or smoke in a work area where hazardous materials are present. Always wash hands before eating. Food should be stored in the welfare cabin — not in work areas. Contaminated food and drink is a real route of exposure to lead, asbestos fibres and chemical contamination.

Welfare facility maintenance — Welfare facilities are only effective if they are kept clean. Everyone on site is responsible for keeping the welfare cabin tidy. Report any defects — broken toilets, no soap, no hot water — to the site manager immediately. Do not accept poor welfare standards.

title: Hand-Arm Vibration (HAVS)
introduction: Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome — HAVS — is a serious and permanent condition caused by using vibrating tools. It affects the blood vessels, nerves and joints in the hands and arms. Symptoms include white or blue fingers in the cold, tingling and numbness, pain and loss of grip strength. Thousands of construction workers have had to leave the industry because of it. The frustrating thing is that it is entirely preventable if we manage exposure correctly.
key_message: Vibration white finger and HAVS are permanent and painful. Once the damage is done it cannot be reversed.
key_points: What causes HAVS — Regular use of vibrating tools — angle grinders, disc cutters, breakers, chipping hammers, plate compactors, scabblers and needle guns. The higher the vibration level and the longer the exposure, the greater the risk. Cold conditions make it worse.

The exposure limits — The Control of Vibration at Work Regulations 2005 set an Exposure Action Value (EAV) of 2.5 m/s² and an Exposure Limit Value (ELV) of 5 m/s². Above the EAV, controls must be in place. The ELV must never be exceeded. Your supervisor has access to tool vibration data and daily exposure calculations.

Controlling exposure — Rotate tasks — do not let one person use a vibrating tool all day. Use lower vibration alternatives where available. Keep tools maintained — blunt cutting tools vibrate more. Use anti-vibration gloves where specified. Take regular breaks from vibrating tools — at least 10 minutes in every hour of use.

Keep warm and dry — Cold reduces blood flow to the fingers and dramatically worsens the effects of vibration. Wear warm gloves when working in cold conditions. Keep hands warm during breaks. Report any numbness or colour changes in fingers to your supervisor — especially in cold weather.

Health surveillance — If you regularly use vibrating tools, you must be included in health surveillance — regular health checks to detect early signs of HAVS. Report any symptoms immediately — early detection prevents further damage. Never ignore tingling, numbness or colour changes in your fingers.

title: Lifting Operations and Equipment
audience: Plant operators, appointed persons, slinger signallers, all near lifting operations
introduction: Lifting operations are among the highest risk activities on a construction site. Cranes, telehandlers, excavators used as cranes, hoists, gin wheels and chain blocks are all lifting equipment covered by LOLER — the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998. Every year people are killed by falling loads, overturned cranes and failures of lifting equipment. Today we are covering what everyone on site needs to know about staying safe around lifting operations.
key_message: Never stand under a suspended load. A dropped load kills instantly — and it happens without warning.
key_points: LOLER — the law — All lifting equipment must be thoroughly examined by a competent person every 6 months for equipment used to lift people and every 12 months for other lifting equipment — or after any incident. All lifting accessories — slings, shackles, eyebolts — must also be examined every 6 months. Check the current examination certificate before using any lifting equipment.

The Appointed Person — Every lifting operation must be planned and supervised by an Appointed Person — someone trained and competent to plan lifts. For complex lifts, a written lift plan must be produced. The Appointed Person is responsible for the safe execution of every lift. Nobody should carry out an unplanned lift.

Slinger Signaller — The person who attaches loads and gives signals to the crane operator must be a trained and certificated Slinger Signaller (CPCS A40 or equivalent). They are responsible for checking the load, selecting and inspecting the correct lifting accessory and giving clear, agreed signals. Nobody else should signal to a crane operator.

Safe Working Load — The Safe Working Load of every piece of lifting equipment and every lifting accessory must never be exceeded. Check the SWL marked on the equipment before every lift. Slings must be rated for the angle at which they are used — the SWL reduces significantly at wider angles. When in doubt, use a lower angle or more slings.

Exclusion zones — An exclusion zone must be established under and around every crane lift. Nobody should stand under a suspended load under any circumstances. The exclusion zone must be physically enforced — not just communicated verbally. Banksmen control access to the zone.

title: Scaffolding and Access Equipment
audience: All site operatives working from or near scaffold
introduction: Scaffold failures and falls from scaffold kill and seriously injure construction workers every year. The majority of incidents happen not because scaffold was poorly erected, but because it was altered, overloaded, damaged or used without being inspected. Today we are going to cover what every person on this site needs to check before using scaffold, and what to do if something does not look right.
key_message: Scaffold is only safe if it has been inspected and signed off. Check the tag before you step on it.
key_points: The CISRS inspection tag — Every section of scaffold on this site must have a current CISRS inspection tag. The tag is completed by a competent scaffold inspector after inspection — which must happen every 7 days and after any event that might affect stability such as high winds or an impact. Before stepping onto any scaffold, find the tag and check the date. If there is no tag or it is out of date — do not use the scaffold and report it immediately.

What to look for — Before using scaffold check: all boards are fully boarded with no gaps, no damaged or rotten boards, guard rails are at least 950mm high, a mid-rail is in place, toe boards are fitted, the scaffold is tied to the building at correct intervals, standards are plumb and not damaged, and access ladders are secure and extend 1 metre above the landing.

Loading — Scaffold has a maximum load capacity — typically 1.5 kN per square metre for general purpose scaffold. Do not stack excessive materials on scaffold boards. One pack of tiles on a standard scaffold is very different to stacking three packs. If you are unsure about loading, ask the scaffolding contractor before placing materials.

Never alter scaffold — Under no circumstances should any non-scaffolder alter, dismantle or add to a scaffold. Removing a guard rail to make access easier, removing a tie to open a window, adding an extra board — these all compromise the structural integrity of the scaffold. If a change is needed, contact the scaffold contractor.

Mobile scaffold towers — PASMA towers must be erected and dismantled only by trained operatives. Castors must be locked before any person ascends. Outriggers or stabilisers must be deployed. Access is by internal ladder only — through the trapdoor. Never move a tower with a person on it. Maximum height-to-base ratio must be observed.

title: Drugs and Alcohol
introduction: Construction is one of the most dangerous working environments there is. Every task carries risk. Every decision matters. Being under the influence of alcohol or drugs — including prescription medication that impairs your ability — makes every risk dramatically higher. It slows your reactions, affects your judgement and reduces your ability to recognise danger. Today we are covering the company policy and what it means for everyone on this site.
key_message: Coming to site under the influence of drugs or alcohol puts your life and everyone else's at risk. It will not be tolerated.
key_points: The policy — This company operates a zero tolerance policy on alcohol and drugs on site. No person is permitted to work on site while under the influence of alcohol, illegal drugs or any medication that impairs their ability to work safely. Arriving at site under the influence will result in immediate removal from site and may result in dismissal.

The morning after — Alcohol consumed the evening before can still impair performance the following morning. A person who consumed alcohol until midnight may still be over the drink-drive limit — and significantly impaired — at 7am. If you are not sure whether you are fit to work, do not come in. Call your supervisor before you arrive on site.

Prescription medication — Some prescription and over-the-counter medications cause drowsiness and impairment that are just as dangerous as alcohol. If you are taking medication that carries a warning about driving or operating machinery, speak to your supervisor before starting work. This is not about penalising people — it is about keeping them safe.

Testing — This site operates a drug and alcohol testing policy. Operatives may be tested on arrival, randomly during the working day or following any incident or near miss. Refusal to take a test will be treated the same as a positive result. Testing is carried out professionally and confidentially.

Support is available — Alcohol and drug dependency are serious health conditions, not personal failures. If you have a problem, speak to your supervisor or HR in confidence. Support and referral to specialist services is available. Coming forward before an incident is very different from being caught.

title: Mental Health and Wellbeing
introduction: We talk a lot about physical safety on site — and rightly so. But mental health is just as important and far less often talked about. Construction workers are three times more likely to die by suicide than in a workplace accident. The industry has the highest suicide rate of any sector in the UK. Stress, financial pressure, long hours, time away from family, physical pain and job insecurity all take a toll. Today we are creating space to talk about it — because talking saves lives.
key_message: Construction has the highest suicide rate of any industry in the UK. It is okay to talk. We look out for each other on this site.
key_points: The scale of the problem — Around two construction workers die by suicide every working day in the UK. Many more suffer in silence with depression, anxiety and stress. The culture of the industry — tough it out, do not show weakness, get on with it — makes it worse. That culture has to change, and it changes one conversation at a time.

Recognising the signs — In yourself: persistent low mood, difficulty sleeping, loss of interest in things you used to enjoy, feeling hopeless or worthless, increased use of alcohol, withdrawing from friends and family, difficulty concentrating. In a colleague: becoming quieter or more withdrawn, mood changes, taking more risks than usual, giving things away, talking about being a burden.

Starting the conversation — If you are worried about a colleague, ask. A simple direct question — 'Are you okay? You have not seemed yourself lately' — can open a door. You do not need to have all the answers. You just need to listen. Do not worry about saying the wrong thing — saying something is almost always better than saying nothing.

Getting help — Lighthouse Construction Industry Charity provides free, confidential 24-hour support for construction workers and their families: call or text 0345 605 1956 or visit lighthouseclub.org. Samaritans: 116 123 (free, 24 hours). Your GP is also an important first step. You do not have to be in crisis to ask for help.

This is not weakness — Asking for help when you are struggling takes more strength than staying silent. Looking out for a colleague who is not okay is a sign of professionalism. On this site, we look after each other. Mental health is no different from a broken arm — you would not tell someone to walk it off.

title: Permits to Work
introduction: A permit to work is a formal written system used to control high-risk activities on site. It confirms that the right precautions are in place before anyone starts work. Permits are used for activities where the consequences of getting it wrong are severe — working on live electrical systems, confined space entry, hot works, working on pressurised systems, breaking into live services. Today we are covering why permits exist, how they work and why you must never bypass one.
key_message: A permit to work is not paperwork — it is the control that keeps you alive. Never bypass it.
key_points: What requires a permit on this site — On this site, permits to work are required for: hot works, confined space entry, working on or near live electrical systems, breaking into live services — gas, water, steam. Additional activities may require a permit — check with your supervisor before starting any high-risk task that is not covered by standard RAMS.

How a permit works — A permit is issued by a competent, authorised person. It describes the work to be done, the hazards, the precautions that must be in place before work starts, the people authorised to carry out the work, the time period it covers and the sign-off procedure on completion. All of these sections must be completed. A partially completed permit is not valid.

Before work starts — The permit issuer must confirm that all precautions are in place before signing the permit. The person carrying out the work must read and understand the permit, confirm that conditions match what the permit describes, and sign to accept responsibility for carrying out the work safely within its terms.

During the work — The conditions described in the permit must be maintained throughout the work. If conditions change — an unexpected hazard is found, the isolation is disturbed, a different person needs to continue the work — the work must stop and a new permit issued or the existing one revalidated.

Closing the permit — On completion, the permit must be formally closed by the permit issuer. This involves confirming the work is complete, the area is safe, all persons are accounted for, all tools and equipment are removed and any isolations are restored. A closed permit is kept on file for audit purposes.

title: Site Housekeeping
introduction: Poor site housekeeping causes accidents, slows work down, creates fire risks and reflects badly on everyone working here. A site where materials are stored correctly, walkways are clear, waste is managed and tools are put away is a site where people work safely and efficiently. Today we are setting the standard for how this site will be run — and everyone here is responsible for maintaining it.
key_message: A tidy site is a safe site, a productive site and a professional site. Housekeeping is everyone's responsibility — not just the labourer's.
key_points: Clear as you go — The best housekeeping is done during the work, not at the end of the day. Generate waste — put it in the skip. Cut a piece of timber — put the off-cut in the skip, not the floor. Finish with a tool — put it away. This takes no extra time and prevents hazards from building up.

Material storage — Materials must be stored in designated areas — not in walkways, not blocking fire exits, not on scaffold platforms beyond the safe loading limit. Timber and sheet materials must be stored on bearers off the ground and protected from weather. Heavy materials must be stored at ground level or on designated storage areas — not stacked unsafely.

Waste management — This site has designated skips for different waste streams: general waste, timber, metal and hazardous waste. Put waste in the correct skip. Hazardous waste — COSHH substances, asbestos, contaminated materials — must be disposed of correctly with the correct documentation. Do not mix hazardous waste with general waste.

Tool storage — Tools left on site overnight must be stored securely — locked in a van, container or tool store. Do not leave tools on scaffold, in trenches or in areas where they could be a hazard to others or be stolen. Power tool cables must be coiled and stored — not left trailing across the site.

End of day — Before leaving site each day, clear your work area. All waste to skips. Tools stored. Materials covered or secured. Excavations fenced. Scaffold access secured. A five-minute tidy at the end of the day makes the next morning safer and more productive for everyone.

title: Young Workers on Site
audience: All site operatives — particularly supervisors and those working alongside young workers
introduction: Young workers — those under 18, apprentices and those new to the industry — are statistically far more likely to be injured on construction sites than experienced workers. This is not because they are less capable. It is because they lack experience, may not recognise hazards that an experienced person takes for granted, and may feel uncomfortable speaking up when something does not seem right. Today we are talking about how we look after the young and new workers on this site.
key_message: Young workers are more vulnerable on site. They need more supervision, more explanation and more patience — not less.
key_points: The legal position — Workers under 18 have additional legal protections. They must not be employed on work that is beyond their physical or psychological capacity, involves harmful exposure to substances or radiation, involves risk of accident which they are unlikely to recognise due to lack of experience. A specific risk assessment must be carried out for young workers before they start.

Induction and supervision — Young workers must receive a thorough induction that goes beyond what experienced workers receive. They must be supervised more closely, especially in the early weeks. Supervision does not mean standing over them — it means being available, checking in regularly and making sure they feel able to ask questions.

Hazard recognition — Experienced workers recognise dangers instinctively because they have encountered them before. Young workers have not. They need to be shown — not just told — what the hazards are and how to control them. Take time to explain why rules exist, not just what they are. Understanding the reason makes people more likely to follow the rule.

Speaking up — Young workers are least likely to speak up when something does not seem right. They fear being seen as weak, difficult or incompetent. Create an environment where questions are welcomed and concerns can be raised without ridicule. If a young worker raises a concern — take it seriously. They may have spotted something everyone else missed.

Peer pressure — Young workers are most likely to take risks when they feel pressure from peers — to keep up, to prove themselves, to not slow the job down. Never pressure a young worker to skip a safety check or work at a pace that compromises their safety. If you see this happening, intervene.

title: Lone Working
audience: All operatives who may work alone or in isolated areas
introduction: Lone working means working in a location where you cannot be seen or heard by another person, or where you would not receive assistance quickly if something went wrong. On a construction site this includes working in remote areas of a large site, in plant rooms, roof voids, basement areas, after hours, or in isolated buildings. Lone working itself is not illegal, but it must be risk assessed and managed. Today we are covering what you need to do before working alone and how we stay in contact.
key_message: If something goes wrong when you are working alone, no one will know. Plan every lone working situation before you start.
key_points: When is lone working high risk — Some tasks should never be done alone. These include: confined space entry, work on live electrical systems, work at height without edge protection, use of hazardous substances in enclosed areas, and any task where if something went wrong, the consequences would be severe before help could arrive. If in doubt, ask for a second person.

Tell someone — Before starting any lone working, tell your supervisor or a colleague: where you are going, what you are doing, when you expect to be back and what to do if they have not heard from you by a specific time. This is not bureaucracy — if you are injured and cannot call for help, this information is what triggers a search.

Communication — Ensure you have a means of communication throughout the lone working period. Mobile phone signal may not be available in basements, plant rooms or remote sites. Check signal before you start. Agree a radio channel with your supervisor. In areas with no signal, agree a check-in system at intervals.

Check-in procedure — This site uses the following lone working check-in procedure: [INSERT PROCEDURE]. If a lone worker misses a check-in, the supervisor will attempt contact. If no contact is made within [INSERT TIME], the emergency procedure will be activated. All lone workers must know this procedure before starting.

Personal safety — Construction sites also carry risks of personal safety in terms of security — particularly on renovation or remote sites. Trust your instincts. If a situation feels unsafe — leave. Do not confront individuals who should not be on site. Call the police and notify your supervisor. Personal safety always comes before protecting materials or equipment.

title: Struck by Falling Objects
introduction: Being struck by a falling object is one of the most common causes of fatal and serious injury on construction sites. Tools, bricks, timber, fittings — anything dropped from height becomes a potentially lethal projectile. A 1kg hammer dropped from 5 metres hits with a force equivalent to a small car crash. Today we are covering what every person working at height and every person working below must do to prevent this.
key_message: A tool dropped from 5 metres hits the ground with the force of a car travelling at 50mph. Protect the people below you.
key_points: Exclusion zones — Wherever work is being carried out at height, an exclusion zone must be established at ground level below. This must be physically enforced with Heras fencing, barriers and signage — not just cones. The size of the zone must account for the maximum potential trajectory of a dropped object. If people must work below, a scaffold fan or debris netting must be installed.

Toe boards — Every working platform on scaffold must have toe boards fitted — minimum 150mm high. Toe boards prevent tools and materials from rolling off platform edges. They must be in place at all times during work and must be inspected as part of the scaffold inspection. Missing toe boards are a serious defect — report them immediately.

Tool tethering — Any hand tool used at height should be tethered to the operative or the structure with a tool lanyard rated for the tool's weight. Tethered tools cannot fall. This is particularly important for frequently used tools on high-level platforms or MEWP baskets. Specialist tool tethering kits are available for most common site tools.

Secure materials — Any materials stored on scaffold or at height must be secured against movement — particularly in windy conditions. Do not leave loose materials on scaffold overnight. At end of shift, return materials to a safe location or secure them against wind. Bricks, tiles, blocks and fixings must not be left where they could be knocked off.

Hard hats — Hard hats protect against falling objects. But only if they are worn correctly — not on the back of the head, not without the suspension adjusted and not if they are cracked or beyond their service life. On this site, hard hats are mandatory for all persons in all areas unless inside a completely enclosed, permanent structure.

title: Working in Cold Weather
introduction: Construction is an outdoor industry and work continues through the winter months. Cold weather brings additional risks that are not always taken seriously — slippery surfaces, reduced manual dexterity, cold stress and hypothermia, increased risk of musculoskeletal injury, and material failures. Today we are covering how we manage those risks and keep everyone safe and productive through the colder months.
key_message: Cold weather is not just uncomfortable — it increases the risk of accidents, cold stress and frost damage to work. Plan ahead.
key_points: Cold stress and hypothermia — Prolonged exposure to cold, particularly in wet or windy conditions, leads to cold stress — a condition that reduces concentration, reaction times and physical performance. In severe cases this progresses to hypothermia. Symptoms include intense shivering, confusion, slurred speech, loss of coordination. Anyone showing these symptoms must be taken inside, given warm clothing and warm drinks and seek medical attention.

Slips on icy surfaces — Ice and frost on scaffold boards, ladders, roofs and access routes dramatically increases slip risk. First thing in the morning is the highest risk period. Work at height must be suspended until surfaces have been inspected and, where possible, ice has been removed or treated with grit. Never attempt to clear ice from a roof while standing on it.

Reduced manual dexterity — Cold hands do not grip tools, controls or materials as effectively as warm hands. This increases the risk of dropped tools, poor fixings and loss of control of plant or equipment. Warm gloves must be available and worn. Task rotation to allow hands to warm up between cold tasks.

Protecting the work — Fresh concrete, mortar and plaster are damaged by frost. Fresh concrete must not be placed in temperatures at or below 2°C and falling. New brickwork and mortar must be protected with hessian and polythene overnight. Plaster must not be applied in temperatures below 5°C. Failure to protect wet materials from frost causes expensive defects.

Welfare — Welfare facilities are particularly important in cold weather. Hot drinks must be available and accessible throughout the day. Rest periods inside a warm welfare cabin must be provided. Operatives should never be expected to eat lunch outside in freezing temperatures. Adequate warm, waterproof clothing must be available for all outdoor workers.

title: CDM Regulations Awareness
introduction: The Construction Design and Management Regulations 2015 — CDM 2015 — are the main set of regulations governing health and safety in construction. They apply to virtually every construction project in the UK, from a small domestic extension to a major infrastructure project. Crucially, CDM gives duties to everyone involved in a project — including every operative on site. Today we are covering the key elements that every person working here needs to understand.
key_message: CDM gives everyone on site duties — not just managers. Knowing your role keeps you and others safe and legal.
key_points: Who has duties under CDM — CDM 2015 gives duties to five duty holders: the Client, the Principal Designer, the Principal Contractor, Contractors and Workers. Every person on this site is a Worker under CDM. As a worker you have a duty to cooperate with your employer on health and safety matters, follow reasonable instructions, report anything you consider a danger to health or safety and not interfere with anything provided for health and safety.

The Construction Phase Plan — Every notifiable project must have a Construction Phase Plan — a document produced by the Principal Contractor that sets out how health and safety will be managed on the project. This plan is a live document. You have the right to see it. It covers the management of key site risks, welfare arrangements and emergency procedures.

Welfare — CDM 2015 sets out minimum welfare standards that must be provided on every construction site — regardless of size. These include toilets, washing facilities with hot and cold water, soap and drying, drinking water, rest facilities and changing facilities. If these are not being provided, this is a CDM breach — and you can report it.

Your right to stop work — If you believe that continuing with your work would expose you or others to a risk of serious personal injury, you have the right to stop work. You must report the situation to your supervisor immediately. You cannot be penalised for stopping work in good faith due to a genuine safety concern.

The HSE and enforcement — The Health and Safety Executive enforces CDM 2015. HSE inspectors can visit any site at any time without notice. They can issue improvement notices, prohibition notices and prosecute individuals and companies. Construction companies and individuals have been prosecuted and imprisoned for CDM breaches. Compliance is not optional.

title: Emergency Procedures
audience: All site operatives — essential for all new starters
introduction: Emergencies on construction sites happen. Accidents, fires, service strikes, structural failures, medical emergencies. When they happen, the difference between a controlled response and a chaotic one can be the difference between life and death. The time to learn the emergency procedures is not when the alarm is going off. Today we are making sure every person on this site knows exactly what to do.
key_message: In an emergency, people do what they have practised. Know the procedures now — not when it is happening.
key_points: Fire — get out, stay out, call 999 — If you discover a fire — raise the alarm immediately. Shout, activate the nearest fire alarm point. Do not stop to collect tools or belongings. Do not use lifts. Evacuate to the muster point — which is [INSERT MUSTER POINT LOCATION]. Call 999. Do not re-enter the building or site until the fire service declares it safe. Account for all persons at the muster point.

Serious injury — call 999 first — For any serious injury — loss of consciousness, suspected spinal injury, severe bleeding, suspected heart attack — call 999 immediately. Do not move the casualty unless they are in immediate danger. Administer first aid if trained. Stay with the casualty and keep them as calm and still as possible until the ambulance arrives. The site first aider is [INSERT NAME].

Gas leak — evacuate and call — If you smell gas or suspect a gas leak — do not operate any electrical switches. Evacuate the area immediately — a minimum 25-metre exclusion zone. Call the National Gas Emergency line: 0800 111 999. Call 999. Ventilate if safe to do so — open doors and windows. Do not re-enter until cleared by the gas emergency service.

Service strike — If plant or hand tools strike an underground service — stop work immediately. If gas — evacuate 25 metres and call 0800 111 999 and 999. If electric — do not touch the cable or anything in contact with it, call 999 and the DNO. If water — isolate if possible, protect from flooding, notify the site manager. Never attempt to repair a struck service.

The muster point and roll call — The muster point for this site is [INSERT LOCATION]. On evacuation, all persons must proceed immediately to the muster point. The site manager will carry out a roll call using the site register. Nobody leaves the muster point until accounted for. Nobody re-enters the site until the all-clear is given. Visitors must be accompanied to the muster point.

title: Site Security
introduction: Site security affects everyone on this project. Theft of materials and plant costs the construction industry hundreds of millions of pounds every year and has a direct impact on programme, costs and everyone's livelihood. But the safety risk of poor security is even more serious. An unauthorised person on site — a member of the public, a child, a trespasser — who encounters a hazard they do not understand is at severe risk of injury. Today we are covering how we secure this site and why it matters.
key_message: Poor site security leads to theft, vandalism and unauthorised access. An unknown person on site is a danger to themselves and everyone else.
key_points: Access control — Only authorised persons should be on this site. Every person entering must sign in at the site register, produce evidence of identity and induction status, and wear the appropriate PPE. Visitors must be signed in, issued a visitor's helmet and hi-vis vest, and accompanied by a site operative at all times. Challenge anyone you do not recognise — politely but firmly.

Challenging strangers — If you see someone on site who you do not recognise and who does not appear to have a valid reason to be there, challenge them politely. 'Hi, can I help you? Who are you here to see?' is enough. If the person becomes aggressive or refuses to identify themselves, do not confront them physically. Notify the site manager immediately.

Securing the site — At the end of every working day, the site must be secured. Hoarding and fencing must be checked for damage and repaired. All gates and access points must be locked. Plant keys must be removed and stored securely. Fuel tanks must be locked. Valuable materials and tools must be stored in a secure container. Alarm systems must be activated.

Reporting theft and damage — Any theft or damage must be reported to the site manager immediately. Do not assume it is minor or not worth reporting. A single missing item can indicate a larger problem. Report even near misses — finding a fence panel moved, a gate unlocked or signs of attempted access. Early reporting can prevent further loss.

Personal valuables — Do not bring valuable personal items to site — expensive jewellery, large amounts of cash, high-value personal tools. The company cannot be held responsible for personal items that are lost or stolen on site. Secure your personal tools in a locked van or container when not in use. Do not leave valuables visible in vehicles parked near the site.

title: Environmental Awareness on Site
introduction: Construction has a significant impact on the environment — water pollution, air pollution, noise, waste, damage to ecology and protected species. Environmental regulations in the UK are strict and the penalties for non-compliance are severe. The Environment Agency can shut down a site immediately and prosecute individuals as well as companies. Today we are covering the key environmental risks on this site and what every operative is responsible for.
key_message: Environmental damage from construction sites can result in prosecution, massive fines and project shutdown. We all have a responsibility.
key_points: Water pollution — Concrete washout, silt-laden water, fuel and oil, cement and paint washings — these must never enter a watercourse, drain or sewer without consent. Even a small fuel spill that reaches a drain can cause a significant pollution incident and result in prosecution. Spill kits must be on site at all times. Any spillage must be contained and cleaned up immediately.

Waste management — All waste must be managed in accordance with the Site Waste Management Plan. Waste must be segregated, stored correctly and removed by a licensed carrier. Fly-tipping — dumping waste off site without proper disposal — is a criminal offence. The site waste transfer notes must be kept for a minimum of three years. Burning waste on site is prohibited.

Dust and air quality — Construction dust must be managed to protect air quality and avoid nuisance to neighbours. Wheel washing where vehicles leave the site on to public roads. Water suppression on cutting, demolition and earthworks. Covering skips and material stockpiles. Monitoring of dust complaints from neighbours — any complaint must be investigated and acted on.

Protected species — Bats, nesting birds, great crested newts and other protected species may be present on construction sites. Disturbance of protected species is a criminal offence — even without a licence. If any wildlife is discovered during works — particularly nests or roosts — stop work in that area immediately and notify the site manager. A licensed ecologist must be consulted.

Noise and nuisance — Construction noise must be managed to comply with planning conditions and the Environmental Protection Act. Noisy operations should be restricted to agreed working hours. Neighbours must be given advance notice of particularly noisy operations. Complaints from neighbours must be taken seriously — an unresolved complaint can result in a noise abatement notice and work stoppage.

Waste correctly segregated and stored in labelled skips
